course.title: Weather & Meteorology
course.description: A hands-on tour of the science of weather — from the layers of the atmosphere to fronts, storms, and forecasting. Structure adapted from the CK-12 Earth Science (Weather & Climate) sequence (CC BY-NC 3.0).

questions.prompt: Meteorology is best defined as the scientific study of…
questions.explanation: Meteorology studies the atmosphere and the weather it produces — see 'The atmosphere'.

questions.prompt: Which gas makes up roughly 78% of dry air?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is ~78% and oxygen ~21% — see 'Layers of the atmosphere'.

questions.prompt: The layer of the atmosphere where nearly all weather occurs is the…
questions.explanation: The troposphere holds most water vapor and weather — see 'The atmosphere'.

questions.prompt: Wind is air moving from…
questions.explanation: Air flows down the pressure gradient, high to low — see 'Pressure & wind'.

questions.prompt: Clouds form mainly when air…
options: rises, cools, and reaches its dew point
questions.explanation: Rising air cools until vapor condenses — see 'Humidity & clouds'.

questions.prompt: A boundary between two different air masses is called a…
questions.explanation: Fronts are air-mass boundaries — see 'Air masses & fronts'.

questions.prompt: Hurricanes get their energy mainly from…
options: warm ocean water and its evaporation
questions.explanation: Warm water (about 26°C+) fuels evaporation and latent heat release — see 'Storms'.

questions.prompt: On a weather map, lines connecting points of equal pressure are called…
questions.explanation: Isobars connect equal pressures; tight spacing means strong wind — see 'Weather maps'.

lessons.title: The atmosphere and its layers
lessons.grammar_note: Order the layers low-to-high: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the gases in the air and the four main layers of the atmosphere, and say where weather happens. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which single gas makes up most of the air you breathe?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Dry air is about 78% *nitrogen*, 21% *oxygen*, and 1% other gases (argon, carbon dioxide, and traces). Water vapor is separate and varies a lot. The atmosphere is layered by how temperature changes with height: the *troposphere* (surface up to ~12 km) is where nearly all weather occurs and where temperature falls with height; the *stratosphere* holds the *ozone layer* and warms with height; above it lie the *mesosphere* (coldest layer, where meteors burn up) and the *thermosphere* (very hot, very thin, home to auroras).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Why do jet airliners cruise near 11 km? That is the top of the troposphere, just into the calm, stable stratosphere — above most storms and turbulence. Notice this tells you the troposphere is thin: if Earth were an apple, the weather layer would be thinner than the skin.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each: (1) Which layer contains the ozone that absorbs UV? (2) In which layer do you live and see clouds? (3) Which layer is coldest? (4) Does temperature rise or fall as you climb through the troposphere? Answers: (1) stratosphere, (2) troposphere, (3) mesosphere, (4) it falls.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the air is mostly oxygen (it is mostly nitrogen). Mistake: assuming it always gets colder with height (it reverses in the stratosphere). Exit: (a) Percent of air that is nitrogen? (b) The weather layer's name? Answers: about 78%; troposphere.

lessons.title: Temperature, pressure, and wind
lessons.grammar_note: Wind blows from HIGH pressure toward LOW pressure.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how uneven heating creates pressure differences and how those differences drive wind. Warm-up: does air flow from high pressure to low, or the other way?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Sun heats Earth unevenly, so some air warms, expands, and rises, lowering the surface *air pressure* beneath it; cooler air sinks, raising pressure. *Wind* is simply air flowing from high pressure toward low pressure to even out the difference. The steeper the *pressure gradient* (the faster pressure changes over distance), the stronger the wind. Earth's rotation adds the *Coriolis effect*, which curves large-scale winds — to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A sea breeze: on a sunny afternoon land heats faster than water, so air over land rises and its surface pressure drops. Cooler, higher-pressure air over the sea flows inland to replace it — you feel a breeze off the water. At night the land cools faster and the flow reverses into a land breeze.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each: (1) Rising warm air leaves behind high or low surface pressure? (2) Which way does wind blow relative to pressure? (3) Tightly packed isobars mean strong or weak wind? (4) In the Northern Hemisphere, Coriolis curves wind to the right or left? Answers: (1) low, (2) high to low, (3) strong, (4) right.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking warm air sinks (it rises because it is less dense). Mistake: expecting wind to flow low-to-high. Exit: (a) What drives wind? (b) Warm air rises or sinks? Answers: a pressure-gradient difference; it rises.

lessons.title: Humidity, clouds, and precipitation
lessons.grammar_note: Dew point = the temperature at which air becomes saturated and vapor condenses.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Connect humidity, the dew point, cloud formation, and precipitation. Warm-up: what has to happen to rising air for a cloud to appear?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Humidity* is the amount of water vapor in the air; *relative humidity* is how full the air is compared with the most it can hold at that temperature. Warm air holds more vapor than cold air. When air is cooled to its *dew point*, it becomes saturated (100% relative humidity) and vapor *condenses* onto tiny particles to form cloud droplets. Rising air cools this way, which is why clouds form aloft. When droplets grow heavy enough, they fall as *precipitation* — rain, or snow if the air is cold enough.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Why does dew appear on grass overnight? After sunset the ground cools, chilling the air just above it. If that air cools to its dew point, its vapor condenses on the grass as dew. If the surface is below freezing instead, the same process deposits frost — no rain required, just cooling to saturation.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each: (1) Warm air holds more or less vapor than cold air? (2) At the dew point, relative humidity equals what percent? (3) Condensation needs what besides cooling? (4) Cooling air is more likely to form a cloud when it rises or sinks? Answers: (1) more, (2) 100%, (3) tiny particles (condensation nuclei), (4) rises.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking clouds are water vapor (vapor is invisible; clouds are condensed liquid droplets or ice). Mistake: confusing humidity with temperature. Exit: (a) Name for the temperature where air saturates. (b) Do clouds form in rising or sinking air? Answers: the dew point; rising.

lessons.title: Air masses and fronts
lessons.grammar_note: Cold front = cold air pushes under warm; warm front = warm air rides over cold.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe air masses and predict the weather when a cold or warm front passes. Warm-up: what do we call the boundary where two different air masses meet?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An *air mass* is a large body of air with fairly uniform temperature and humidity, taking on the character of the region where it forms (cold and dry over polar land, warm and moist over tropical ocean). Where two air masses meet, the boundary is a *front*. At a *cold front*, dense cold air wedges under warm air, shoving it up steeply — often bringing brief, heavy showers or thunderstorms and a temperature drop. At a *warm front*, warm air glides gently up over retreating cold air, giving a long spell of layered clouds and steady, lighter rain.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Predicting from a front: a station reports falling temperatures, a wind shift, a sudden pressure rise, and a line of towering clouds. That signature is a cold front passing — expect a short, intense burst of rain and clearer, cooler air behind it. Contrast a warm front, where you would first see high wispy cirrus, then thickening, lowering clouds, then hours of gentle rain and rising temperature.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each: (1) Which front usually brings brief, heavy storms? (2) Which brings long, steady, lighter rain? (3) After a cold front passes, is it warmer or cooler? (4) At a warm front, warm air rides over or under the cold air? Answers: (1) cold front, (2) warm front, (3) cooler, (4) over.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a 'cold front' means it is cold now — it means colder air is arriving. Mistake: assuming every front brings the same rain. Exit: (a) What is a front? (b) Which front slopes steeply and storms? Answers: a boundary between two air masses; the cold front.

lessons.title: Storms: thunderstorms, hurricanes, and tornadoes
lessons.grammar_note: Thunderstorms need warm, moist, rising unstable air; hurricanes need warm ocean water.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what powers thunderstorms, hurricanes, and tornadoes, and how they differ in size. Warm-up: what ocean condition does a hurricane need to grow?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A *thunderstorm* forms when warm, moist air rises rapidly in an unstable atmosphere, building a tall *cumulonimbus* cloud; as vapor condenses it releases *latent heat* that fuels stronger updrafts, and charge separation produces lightning and thunder. A *hurricane* is a huge, organized system of thunderstorms spiraling around a low-pressure *eye*; it draws energy from warm ocean water (about 26°C or warmer) and weakens over land or cold water. A *tornado* is a small but violent rotating column of air stretching from a strong storm's base to the ground, with the fastest winds on Earth over a narrow path.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Why do hurricanes fade after landfall? Cut off from the warm water that supplied evaporating vapor and latent heat, the engine loses its fuel, and friction over land disrupts the circulation — so wind speeds drop even as heavy rain and flooding continue inland. This is why forecasters track a storm's position relative to warm water so closely.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each: (1) Which storm is largest in size? (2) Which has the single fastest winds over a narrow path? (3) What ocean temperature roughly does a hurricane need? (4) What cloud type produces thunderstorms? Answers: (1) hurricane, (2) tornado, (3) about 26°C or warmer, (4) cumulonimbus.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking hurricanes strengthen over land (they weaken without warm water). Mistake: confusing a hurricane's broad scale with a tornado's narrow one. Exit: (a) What fuels a hurricane? (b) Rising air in a storm releases what kind of heat as vapor condenses? Answers: warm ocean water; latent heat.

lessons.title: Applied project: forecast your local weather

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Act as a forecaster: predict the weather where you live for the next three days and explain your reasoning using the concepts from this course. You are not just guessing a number — you are showing the atmospheric logic behind each call.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Record today's conditions: temperature, sky (clouds), wind direction, and whether pressure is rising or falling. 2) Identify any front or pressure system that may be approaching and say which way it is moving. 3) Write a day-by-day forecast for the next three days (temperature trend, cloud/precipitation, wind). 4) For each day, justify the prediction: e.g. 'a cold front is approaching from the west, so I expect a brief thunderstorm then cooler, clearer air.'

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ You reported real starting conditions including a pressure trend. ✔ You named a front or high/low pressure system and its direction of motion. ✔ Each day's forecast covers temperature, precipitation, and wind. ✔ Every prediction is justified with a cause (pressure change, front type, humidity, or warm/cold air). If all four are true, you are reasoning like a meteorologist.
